opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so a lot of kernel work is honestly not the glamorous part. The core idea, like how you tile the attention computation or how you overlap memory loads with compute, might take a few days of thinking. Then there are weeks of everything else: boilerplate, getting the indexing right, handling all the edge cases for different head dimensions and sequence lengths, writing tests, benchmarking scripts, porting things between hardware generations. That's where I've found tools like Claude Code really helpful.

What's nice is that it can operate in the actual repo. It reads the existing kernels, understands the conventions we use, and then I can say, "Add support for this variant," or "Write a test that compares this against the reference PyTorch implementation across these shapes." It'll go do that, run it, see what fails, and iterate. That loop of write, compile, test, fix is exactly what eats up a lot of time in kernel development.

I'd say it's not at the point where it invents the next FlashAttention on its own. The really hard part is still understanding the hardware deeply: where the bottleneck is, whether you're memory-bound or compute-bound, how to schedule things across warps. But it's surprisingly good at being a very fast, tireless collaborator on everything around that. It also lowers the barrier for people who want to get into this area. Writing high-performance kernels used to require a lot of tribal knowledge. Now someone can ask questions about the code, get things explained, and get to a working version much faster.

So for me it's mostly a productivity multiplier. I spend more of my time on the ideas and less on the plumbing, and that's been a pretty big shift.

r001.rationale: The response describes the central kernel work as hardware-aware choices—tiling attention, overlapping memory loads with compute, identifying bottlenecks, and scheduling across warps—and says this remains the hard part.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it surprised me a bit, because kernel work is the part of my job I assumed would be hardest to delegate. Writing a fast attention kernel is mostly about understanding the hardware: how the memory hierarchy behaves, what the tensor cores want, where you're stalling on shared memory bank conflicts or register pressure. That's deep, specialized knowledge, and I didn't expect a model to be that useful there.

Where it turned out to help most is everything around the core idea. Once I know what I want the kernel to do, there's an enormous amount of tedious, error-prone work: writing the launch boilerplate, handling all the shape and dtype variants, writing correctness tests against a reference PyTorch implementation, building out the benchmarking harness so I can actually see whether a change moved the needle. Claude Code is very good at that. I can describe the structure I want, and it produces something I can iterate on in minutes instead of spending an afternoon on it.

The second thing is debugging. With CUDA, when something goes wrong, you often get a very unhelpful error, or worse, you get silently wrong numbers. Being able to say "here's the kernel, here's the test that fails, here are the indices where the output diverges," and have it reason through the indexing with me, has saved a lot of time. It's not always right, but it's a good second pair of eyes, and it's fast at generating hypotheses I can go verify.

And then there's the exploration side. When I'm trying out a new idea, say a different tiling strategy or a new way to pipeline loads with compute, I want to try several variants quickly and just measure. Having an agent that can write out the variants, run them, and report back the numbers lets me stay at the level of "what's the right algorithmic structure" rather than getting bogged down in each implementation.

I'd say the bottom line is that it doesn't replace understanding the hardware. If you don't know why you're doing something, it won't save you. But it compresses the loop between having an idea and finding out if the idea was good, and in performance work that loop is everything.

r001.rationale: The response says fast attention kernels require understanding hardware and mentions exploring tiling and load/compute pipelines, but it does not clearly identify designing architectures to take advantage of hardware as a major focus of Tri Dao’s work.

astra-6.text:
With GPU kernels, there’s a lot of iteration: you write something, check that it’s correct, benchmark it, and try to understand what’s limiting performance. Claude Code is useful because it can help with that whole loop—reading the code, making a change, and running the tests—rather than just suggesting a snippet that I then have to integrate myself.

I still have to guide the optimization and evaluate the results. A change can look reasonable and make the kernel slower. But being able to delegate some of the implementation and testing makes it much easier to try an idea and get feedback.

r001.rationale: The response discusses iterating on, testing, and optimizing GPU kernels, but does not identify designing architectures to take advantage of hardware as a major focus.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find useful is that writing a GPU kernel involves more than the kernel itself. You need a reference implementation, correctness tests, benchmarks, and a way to understand where performance is going. Claude Code can help with that surrounding work, which makes it faster to try an idea.

The key is having a tight feedback loop. You make a change, check that the result is correct, and measure whether it actually gets faster. I still need to reason about the algorithm and how it maps onto the hardware, but having help with implementation and iteration lets me spend more time on those decisions.
